direct_answer:
Aker BP conducted its double materiality assessment (DMA) initially in 2023 under CSRD/ESRS and revised it in 2024 based on new information, implementation guidance and EFRAG’s draft oil & gas sector standard [Source 5]. The DMA included mapping impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), their dependencies, and their connection to Aker BP’s own operations and value chain, and it followed a structured four-step/iterative process (Figure 9) [Source 5][Source 1][Source 9].

Methodologically, the DMA covers both (i) impact materiality (inside-out: impacts from Aker BP’s activities on environment and society) and (ii) financial materiality (outside-in: financial risks/opportunities to the business model and performance, including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources) [Source 2]. IROs are identified using top-down and bottom-up approaches with input from internal and external stakeholders and quantitative sources, then assessed and prioritised using a standardised rating system based on impact and financial materiality criteria [Source 9]. Impact assessments use a severity × likelihood approach aligned with the company’s enterprise risk management scales (and documented in the same tool as risks/opportunities), so IROs are prioritised and handled together with other company risks [Source 2]. Activities, business relationships and geographies are considered; for own operations Aker BP focused on oil and gas production as the activity with the highest potential for material impact, while upstream value chain material topics mainly relate to development projects due to significant construction activity [Source 1]. The DMA incorporates stakeholder perspectives via engagement channels (e.g., PDO impact assessment consultations, whistleblowing channel) and, for the 2024 process, in-depth interviews and workshops with internal management/subject matter experts informed by prior-year interviews with owners, key suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 3]. Outcomes (material IROs) were reviewed by the Board of Directors (BoD), Audit & Risk Committee (ARC) and Executive Management Team (EMT) [Source 8].

Material sustainability matters identified as material include: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, and resource use and circular economy (identified as strategic/highest priority with high impact and high financial relevance) [Source 1]. Affected communities, biodiversity and ecosystems, and workers in the value chain are also considered material (significant impacts and compliance relevance, though comparatively lower financial materiality) [Source 1]. Water and marine resources were assessed as lower overall materiality in the matrix, but Aker BP states that water consumption became material in parts of its upstream value chain in 2024 due to ramp-up of construction activity abroad (though not in own operations) [Source 1][Source 8]. Aker BP also added an entity-specific IRO on cyber attacks and introduced “cyber security” as a governance sub-topic in the updated DMA [Source 8].
compliance_rationale: The passages describe the DMA’s double materiality coverage (inside-out and outside-in), identification and assessment approach (top-down/bottom-up, stakeholder input, severity×likelihood, prioritisation, validation by management/Board), and list the sustainability matters considered material (including changes such as water consumption in upstream value chain and cyber security) [Source 2][Source 9][Source 3][Source 1][Source 8]. However, the evidence does not provide the full detailed four-step process content (Figure 9 steps are referenced but not enumerated in text) nor a complete, explicit list of all material matters/sub-topics as would be expected from the referenced Table 3 of material IROs [Source 1][Source 8].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit description of each of the four steps in the DMA process (Figure 9 is referenced but the step-by-step text is not fully provided in the retrieved passages) [Source 1][Source 5][Source 9].
Complete list of material IROs and the full mapping to sustainability matters/sub-topics/sub-sub-topics (Table 3 is referenced but not included in the retrieved passages) [Source 8].
Clear thresholds/criteria for determining when an impact or financial effect is deemed ‘material’ (beyond noting use of standardised rating and severity×likelihood) [Source 2][Source 9].
Explicit disclosure of where in the upstream/downstream value chain each material matter arises (the text provides examples, but not a comprehensive mapping for all material matters) [Source 1].
key_findings: DMA first performed in 2023 and revised in 2024 using new information, guidance and EFRAG draft oil & gas sector standard [Source 5].
DMA covers both impact materiality (inside-out) and financial materiality (outside-in), including reputational risk and dependencies [Source 2].

IROs identified via top-down and bottom-up approaches with internal/external stakeholder input and quantitative sources; assessed and prioritised using standardised ratings; validated by management and Board [Source 9].
Assessment considers activities, business relationships and geographies; own operations focus on oil & gas production; upstream value chain focus on development projects/construction [Source 1].
Stakeholder perspectives incorporated through engagement channels and interviews/workshops; key stakeholder groups included owners, suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 3].
Material matters (highest priority): climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, resource use & circular economy [Source 1].
Also material: affected communities, biodiversity & ecosystems, workers in the value chain [Source 1].
Water consumption became material in parts of upstream value chain in 2024; cyber security added as an entity-specific governance sub-topic [Source 8].
